summary: Defines a method for turning a name registered in the Domain Name System into an LDAP distinguished name. This gives directories a convenient way to name organizations based on their Internet domain names.

eli5.summary: It shows how to turn a web-style name like example.com into the form a directory uses, so each organization gets an easy-to-find spot.

questions: how to represent a domain name as an ldap dn
what is dc in an ldap distinguished name
how to convert a domain name to an ldap dn
what is the dcobject object class
what is the domain object class in ldap
subtitle: How to turn a DNS domain name into an LDAP distinguished name, one DC component at a time.

tldr.problem: Directories built on X.500 and LDAP need unique names for entries, but there was no established registration infrastructure in many regions to assign and guarantee unique names.
tldr.mechanism: Each component of a domain name becomes a relative distinguished name of the form DC=component, written most significant first, so CS.UCL.AC.UK becomes DC=CS,DC=UCL,DC=AC,DC=UK. The memo also defines the dc attribute and two object classes, dcObject and domain.
tldr.outcome: An enterprise automatically gets a distinguished name for each domain name it already holds. The memo is a Proposed Standard that was later updated by RFC 4519 and RFC 4524.

today: RFC 2247 is a Proposed Standard published in January 1998. It has been updated by RFC 4519 and RFC 4524, so those documents should be read alongside it.

sections.title: Why Domain Names Can Name Directory Entries
sections.content:
The Lightweight Directory Access Protocol (LDAP) identifies each entry by an X.500-compatible distinguished name. The Domain Name System (RFC 1034) also labels things hierarchically, as an ordered set of short string components, such as CRITICAL-ANGLE.COM.

A key difference is that every component of a distinguished name carries an explicit attribute type, while a domain name component does not. X.500 itself does not require any particular naming structure. It suggests structures based on geographic and national regions, but the RFC notes that in many regions there was no established registration infrastructure that could assign names or ensure they were unique.

The mechanism in this memo gives an enterprise a distinguished name for each domain name it has already obtained for use in the Internet. As in a domain name, the most significant component, closest to the root, is written last: DC=CRITICAL-ANGLE,DC=COM.

The memo does not say how to name objects that have no domain name, and does not say how to find an enterprise's LDAP server from its domain name. It leaves such procedures to possible future RFCs.
sections.eli5: Everyone who owns a web-style name already has a unique name. This memo reuses that name so a directory does not need a new naming system.

sections.title: Mapping a Domain Name to a Distinguished Name
sections.content:
The algorithm starts with an empty distinguished name and attaches one relative distinguished name (RDN) for each component of the domain, most significant (rightmost) first. Each RDN is a single attribute type and value pair. The type is the attribute DC, and the value is an IA5 string holding the domain name component.

The mapping works in both directions. Any Internet domain name can be transformed into a distinguished name, and a distinguished name made of one or more RDNs that all contain only the attribute type DC can be mapped back to a domain name.

The memo defines no domain name equivalence for any other kind of distinguished name.
sections.eli5: You read the web name from right to left and write each piece after a label that says DC. You can undo it just as easily.

sections.title: The dc Attribute Type
sections.content:
The DC attribute (short for domainComponent) is defined with the object identifier 0.9.2342.19200300.100.1.25 and the name dc. It uses the IA5 string syntax, case-insensitive equality and substring matching rules, and it is SINGLE-VALUE.

The value is a string holding one component of a domain name. In LDAP the encoding of an IA5String is simply the characters of the string. The equality rule ignores case, matching the case-insensitive behavior of DNS at the time.
sections.eli5: The label DC is a labeled slot that holds exactly one piece of a web name, and it does not care about capital letters.

sections.title: The dcObject and domain Object Classes
sections.content:
An object whose name is derived from its domain name using the algorithm above is an entry in the directory, with the DC attribute present and used as its RDN. An LDAP server only holds an attribute in an entry when the entry's object class permits it, so the memo defines two object classes.

dcObject is an auxiliary class (object identifier 1.3.6.1.4.1.1466.344) that requires dc. It is meant to be added to an entry that already has a suitable structural class, such as organization, organizationalUnit or locality.

domain is a structural class (object identifier 0.9.2342.19200300.100.4.13) that also requires dc. It is for entries where no other information is stored, typically placeholders or domains that do not correspond to real-world entities. It permits a list of optional descriptive attributes, including description, telephoneNumber and postalAddress, which are already defined for LDAP in RFC 2256.

For X.500 servers, the memo also gives a name form rule, domainNameForm, that lets the domain class be named by dc.
sections.eli5: An entry can wear a small badge saying it has a web-name piece (dcObject), or it can be a plain placeholder card (domain) when there is nothing else to say.

sections.title: Example Entries
sections.content:
For an organization, the entry has organization as its structural class and dcObject as an auxiliary class. The RFC's example is the entry dc=critical-angle,dc=com with o: Critical Angle Inc..

For a placeholder, the RFC's example is dc=tcp,dc=critical-angle,dc=com with the structural class domain and the description a placeholder entry used with SRV records.
sections.eli5: A company gets a card with its name on it. A placeholder gets a plain card that just says what it is for.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The memo says it describes how attributes of objects may be discovered and retrieved, so servers should maintain an appropriate security policy.

It also warns that an enterprise is not restricted in what it may store in DNS or LDAP servers. A client that contacts an untrusted server may be given incorrect or misleading information. For example, an organization's server might claim to hold naming contexts for domain names that were never delegated to that organization.
sections.eli5: Just because a directory says it holds a name does not make it true, so be careful which servers you believe.
